note: Prototype catalog picked by hand. It stands in for the daily cloud catalog. Facts checked on 2026-10-15; see research/external/catalog-fact-check-2026-10-15.md.

buckets.name: AI meeting notes
buckets.job: Writes up what was said, so you can pay attention to the person.
buckets.gapLine: You don't have an AI notetaker set up.

buckets.name: Interview practice
buckets.job: Lets you rehearse answers out loud and get feedback before the real thing.
buckets.gapLine: You don't have a way to practice out loud and get feedback.

buckets.name: Reading and research
buckets.job: Answers questions about your readings and shows where it found the answer.
buckets.gapLine: You don't have an AI tool that works from your own readings.

buckets.name: Study and exam prep
buckets.job: Turns your notes into practice questions and explains what you got wrong.
buckets.gapLine: You don't have an AI study tool set up.

buckets.name: Slide drafting
buckets.job: Gets you from an outline to a first draft of slides.
buckets.gapLine: You don't have an AI tool for drafting slides.

buckets.name: Writing feedback
buckets.job: Reads your draft and tells you what's unclear, without writing it for you.
buckets.gapLine: You don't have an AI tool giving you feedback on drafts.

buckets.name: Design and AI
buckets.job: Lets your AI assistant see and work with your design files.
buckets.gapLine: Your AI assistant can't see your Figma files yet.

buckets.name: AI coding agent
buckets.job: Writes and edits code across your project while you review.
buckets.gapLine: You don't have an AI coding agent set up.

tools.name: Granola
tools.cost: Free plan keeps 30 days of notes. Paid plans start at $14 a month, and US students can get Business free for 12 months.
tools.dataAccess: Your mic and your computer's audio while a note is running, plus your calendar to name the notes. The audio goes to Granola's transcription service and isn't saved.
tools.consentNote: Ask before you take AI notes. Some people, including some recruiters, will say no.
tools.why: It runs on your Mac and doesn't send a bot into the call, so a coffee chat still feels like a conversation.
tools.avoidIf: the other person says no to notes.

steps: Install Granola.
Sign in with your Google or Microsoft account so it can see your calendar.
Allow microphone and system audio when macOS asks.

networking: Open Granola a minute before the chat. Your event should already be there.
Ask if it's OK to take notes, then hit Start.
Jot a word or two when something matters, like a name or a next step. Granola fills in the rest.
Afterwards, ask Granola's chat to draft a thank-you email that mentions what you talked about.
default: Open Granola a minute before the meeting. Your event should already be there.
Hit Start when the meeting begins.
Type short notes when something matters. Granola merges them with the transcript.
Afterwards, ask it for the action items and who owns each one.

tools.name: Notion AI Meeting Notes
tools.cost: Needs a Notion Business or Enterprise plan. Free and Plus plans, including the free student plan, only get a short trial.
tools.dataAccess: Your mic and computer audio during the meeting, saved to your Notion workspace.
tools.consentNote: Ask before you take AI notes.
tools.why: If your notes already live in Notion, the transcript and summary land right next to them.
tools.coachLine: You have Notion. If your workspace is on a Business plan, it can take AI meeting notes.

steps: Open the Notion desktop app and type /meet on a new page.
Allow microphone and screen and system audio recording when macOS asks.
Start the notes when the meeting begins.

default: Make a page for the meeting and type /meet.
Start the notes when people start talking.
Afterwards, read the summary and fix anything it got wrong before you share it.

tools.name: Zoom meeting summary
tools.cost: Free with your Yale Zoom account. Free personal Zoom accounts get summaries for 3 hosted meetings a month.
tools.dataAccess: What people say in the meeting, transcribed and summarized by Zoom.
tools.consentNote: Everyone in the call sees a lit AI icon at the top right while the summary runs.
tools.why: Nothing to install if you already meet on Zoom. It summarizes the call and lists next steps.
tools.coachLine: You have Zoom, and it can summarize calls you host. You haven't used it yet.

steps: Sign in at yale.zoom.us with your NetID and open Settings.
Check that meeting summary is on. Yale turns it on by default.
In your next call that you host, click the AI icon at the top right and choose Start Summary.

default: If you're the host, click the AI icon at the top right and choose Start Summary.
Let it run for the whole call.
Check the summary email afterwards and fix the action items before you forward them.

tools.name: Otter
tools.cost: Free plan: 300 minutes a month, and each recording stops at 30 minutes.
tools.dataAccess: The meeting audio. Its assistant can join your calls as a participant.
tools.consentNote: Otter's Notetaker joins as a visible participant, which can feel odd in a 1:1 chat. Yale blocks AI bots like it in Yale Zoom calls.
tools.why: Works in the browser on any computer, and the free plan is enough to try it.

steps: Sign up on otter.ai.
Open it in a browser tab, or in the Otter Mac app, and hit Record when the meeting starts.
Skip the calendar auto-join for Yale Zoom calls, because Yale blocks the bot.

default: Hit Record when the meeting starts.
Highlight lines that matter while it transcribes.
Afterwards, share the summary, not the whole transcript.

tools.name: Big Interview
tools.cost: Free for Yale students through the Office of Career Strategies
tools.dataAccess: Video and audio of your practice answers, stored in your Big Interview account.
tools.why: OCS gives it to Yale students for free. It has question sets by industry and gives feedback on your recorded answers.

steps: Open the Big Interview link on the OCS Big Interview page.
Sign in with your Yale account.
Pick the question set for the role you're interviewing for.

interview: Pick a question set that matches the role.
Record two or three answers out loud. Don't script them.
Watch one back and check the feedback on pace and filler words.
Redo the weakest answer once, then stop. You're warming up, not memorizing.

tools.name: Yoodli
tools.cost: Free for 5 practice sessions in total. Paid plans start at $8 a month, billed yearly.
tools.dataAccess: Your mic and camera while you practice.
tools.why: An AI interviewer asks follow-up questions, so it feels closer to a real conversation.

steps: Sign up on yoodli.ai.
Pick an interview roleplay that matches the role.
Allow mic and camera in your browser.

interview: Start a roleplay for the role you're interviewing for.
Answer out loud like it's real.
Read the feedback on your two longest answers. Long usually means unfocused.

tools.name: Mock interview in ChatGPT voice
tools.cost: Works on the free plan, but free voice time is limited.
tools.dataAccess: What you say and paste into the chat, sent to OpenAI.
tools.why: ChatGPT's voice mode can play the interviewer. Give it the job description and ask it to push back on vague answers.
tools.coachLine: You already have ChatGPT. Its voice mode makes a decent mock interviewer.

steps: Open ChatGPT.

interview: Open ChatGPT and paste in the job description.
Say: interview me for this role, one question at a time, and push back when I'm vague.
Click the Voice icon and answer out loud for 15 minutes. On the free plan you may run out of voice time.
Ask which two answers were weakest and why.

tools.name: Mock interview with Claude
tools.cost: Works on the free plan
tools.dataAccess: What you type or paste into the chat, sent to Anthropic.
tools.why: Claude is good at asking a sharp follow-up when an answer is vague, which is what real interviewers do.
tools.coachLine: You already have Claude. It can run a mock interview with follow-up questions.

steps: Open Claude.

interview: Paste in the job description and your resume.
Say: interview me for this role, one question at a time. Ask a follow-up whenever I'm vague.
Answer each question the way you'd say it out loud.
At the end, ask for the one habit that hurt your answers most.

tools.name: Mock interview in Gemini Live
tools.cost: Works on the free plan
tools.dataAccess: What you say in the conversation, sent to Google.
tools.why: Gemini Live is a back-and-forth voice conversation, so you can practice answering out loud.
tools.coachLine: You already have Gemini. Gemini Live, on your phone or in Chrome, can play the interviewer out loud.

steps: Open the Gemini app on your phone, or click Ask Gemini at the top of Chrome on your Mac.

interview: Start Gemini Live. Tap Live in the phone app, or click Go Live in Gemini in Chrome.
Tell it the role and ask it to interview you, one question at a time.
Ask which answer you should practice again.

tools.name: Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM)
tools.cost: Free with a Google account, including your Yale EliApps account.
tools.dataAccess: The files and links you upload, stored in your Google account.
tools.why: It answers from the sources you give it and cites the exact passage, so it's safer for readings than a general chatbot.

steps: Open Gemini Notebook and sign in with Google. Your Yale account works.
Make a notebook for this course.
Upload the readings as PDFs or paste in links.

reading: Put this week's readings in one notebook.
Ask for the main argument of each one in two sentences.
Click the citations to check it read them right.
Ask where the readings disagree. That's usually the seminar discussion.
lecture: Upload the slides or readings for this class.
Ask for three questions you could raise in section.
Click the citations so you can point to the page if someone asks.
exam: Put your lecture notes and readings in one notebook.
Ask it to make a practice quiz on the topics most likely to come up.
Take the quiz, then ask why each wrong answer was wrong.
Make flashcards from the ones you missed.

tools.name: Perplexity
tools.cost: Free plan, Pro costs extra
tools.dataAccess: Your questions, sent to Perplexity.
tools.why: Good for finding sources fast. Every answer links to where it came from.

steps: Open Perplexity in your browser.
Sign in so it keeps your threads.

default: Ask a specific question, like what changed in a field since a certain year.
Open two or three of the linked sources yourself.
Save the good sources into your own notes.

tools.name: Claude Projects
tools.cost: Works on the free plan, up to 5 projects.
tools.dataAccess: The files you add to the project, stored in your Claude account.
tools.why: Keep a course's readings in one Project, and every chat about that course can use them.
tools.coachLine: You already use Claude. A Project per course keeps your readings ready for every chat.

steps: Open Claude and make a new Project for the course.
Add the readings as files.

default: Make a Project named after the course.
Add the syllabus and this week's readings.
Start chats inside the Project so it uses them.
Ask it to quote the passage it's relying on, then check it.

tools.name: ChatGPT Projects
tools.cost: Works on the free plan, with fewer files per project than paid plans.
tools.dataAccess: The files you add to the project, stored in your ChatGPT account.
tools.why: Group a course's readings and chats in one Project so ChatGPT keeps the context.
tools.coachLine: You already use ChatGPT. A Project per course keeps your readings ready for every chat.

steps: Open ChatGPT and make a new Project.
Add the readings as files.

default: Make a Project named after the course.
Add the syllabus and this week's readings.
Ask questions inside the Project so it uses them.
Ask where in the reading each claim comes from, then check it.

tools.name: Gemini Deep Research
tools.cost: Limited use on the free plan
tools.dataAccess: Your question, sent to Google. It searches the web, and it can also read files you upload.
tools.why: It reads dozens of sources and writes a cited report. Good for background before a seminar.
tools.coachLine: You already have Gemini. Deep Research can write you a cited background brief.

steps: Open Gemini and pick Deep Research.

default: Pick Deep Research and ask a focused question.
Check the research plan before it starts and cut what you don't need.
Open the three sources it leans on most and read those yourself.

tools.name: ChatGPT study mode
tools.cost: Works on the free plan
tools.dataAccess: What you type or upload, sent to OpenAI.
tools.why: Study mode asks you questions instead of handing over answers, which is what actually helps before an exam.
tools.coachLine: You already have ChatGPT. Its study mode quizzes you instead of giving answers away.

steps: Open ChatGPT in a regular chat, click +, and pick Study. It doesn't work inside Projects.

exam: Turn on study mode and upload the exam topics or your notes.
Ask it to quiz you, one question at a time.
When you miss one, ask it to walk you through it with hints, not the answer.
End by asking which topic to review again tonight.

tools.name: Claude learning mode
tools.cost: Check your Claude plan
tools.dataAccess: What you type or upload, sent to Anthropic.
tools.why: Learning mode guides you with questions so you work the problem out yourself.
tools.coachLine: You already have Claude. Its learning mode walks you through problems instead of solving them.

steps: Open Claude. If the style menu has Learning, pick it. If not, ask Claude to quiz you and give hints instead of answers.

exam: Pick the Learning style if you see it, then upload your notes.
Ask it to quiz you on the exam topics.
When you're stuck, ask for a hint, not the answer.

tools.name: Gemini Guided Learning
tools.cost: Works on the free plan
tools.dataAccess: What you type or upload, sent to Google.
tools.why: Guided Learning breaks a topic into steps and checks your understanding as you go.
tools.coachLine: You already have Gemini. Guided Learning can quiz you step by step.

steps: Open gemini.google.com, click +, then More tools, and pick Guided Learning.

exam: Pick Guided Learning and name the exam topic.
Ask for a short practice set on whatever you got wrong.

tools.name: Quizlet
tools.cost: Free plan with a few AI study guides and practice tests. Quizlet Plus starts at $35.99 a year.
tools.dataAccess: The notes you paste in, stored in your Quizlet account.
tools.why: Turns your notes into flashcards and practice tests quickly.

steps: Sign up on quizlet.com.
Paste in your notes to make a set.

exam: Paste in your notes and let it make cards.
Delete cards that are too easy.
Run a practice test the night before, not five minutes before.

tools.name: Gamma
tools.cost: Free plan with 400 AI credits at sign-up and up to 10 slides per prompt.
tools.dataAccess: Your outline and any files you upload.
tools.why: Paste an outline and get a full draft deck in a minute. You still fix the content, but the layout work is done.

steps: Sign up on gamma.app.
Paste your outline into Gamma's chat and ask for a deck.

presentation: Paste your outline or notes into Gamma.
Generate, then delete every slide that doesn't earn its place.
Rewrite each headline as a full sentence that says the point.
Export to PowerPoint or Google Slides if your group uses those.

tools.name: Copilot in PowerPoint
tools.cost: Needs your own Microsoft 365 Personal, Family or Premium plan, or a paid Copilot license. Yale's free Copilot Chat doesn't work inside PowerPoint.
tools.dataAccess: Your slides and any files you point it at, processed by Microsoft.
tools.why: Drafts slides inside PowerPoint, so your group can keep editing in the same file.
tools.coachLine: You have PowerPoint. If your Microsoft 365 plan includes Copilot, it can draft slides from your outline.

steps: Open PowerPoint, start a new presentation, and click the Copilot icon at the bottom right of the slide.

presentation: Click Copilot and paste your outline, then ask for a deck.
Cut slides until each one has a single point.
Ask Copilot to tighten the speaker notes.

tools.name: Canva
tools.cost: Free plan includes up to 20 AI uses. Canva Pro ($144 a year) gives about 10 times more.
tools.dataAccess: Your designs and uploads, stored in your Canva account.
tools.why: Good-looking templates and AI drafting for decks that need to look polished.

steps: Sign up on canva.com.
On the home page, open Canva AI and pick Presentation.

presentation: Use Canva AI to draft a first pass from your outline. Fix the outline before it generates.
Swap stock photos for your own charts or screenshots.

tools.name: Claude
tools.cost: Free plan, Pro for heavier use
tools.dataAccess: Whatever you paste in, sent to Anthropic.
tools.consentNote: Career advisors are wary of AI-written cover letters. Ask for feedback and keep the words yours.
tools.why: Paste a draft and ask what's unclear or generic. It's good at explaining why a sentence is weak.
tools.coachLine: You have Claude, but you haven't opened it lately. It's good at blunt feedback on drafts.

steps: Install the Claude app.
Sign in or make a free account.

writing: Paste your draft and the job posting.
Ask which sentences could be in anyone's cover letter. Tell it not to rewrite them.
Fix those yourself with a specific story or number.
Ask once more for anything that sounds stiff.

tools.name: ChatGPT
tools.cost: Free plan, Plus for heavier use
tools.dataAccess: Whatever you paste in, sent to OpenAI.
tools.consentNote: Career advisors are wary of AI-written cover letters. Ask for feedback and keep the words yours.
tools.why: Paste a draft and ask where a reader would lose interest.
tools.coachLine: You have ChatGPT, but you haven't opened it lately. It can give you feedback on this draft.

steps: Install the ChatGPT app.
Sign in or make a free account.

writing: Paste your draft and the job posting.
Ask where a recruiter would stop reading, and why.
Ask it to check that every claim has an example behind it.

tools.name: Grammarly
tools.cost: Free plan with 100 AI prompts a month. Pro adds full-sentence rewrites.
tools.dataAccess: Text you type in apps where it's turned on. Turn it off for anything private.
tools.why: Catches grammar and tone while you type, in whatever app you're writing in.

steps: Install Grammarly.
Allow Accessibility access when macOS asks, so it can read what you type.

writing: Open your draft. Grammarly underlines what it flags.
Accept grammar fixes, but be picky about tone suggestions.
Read the final version out loud once yourself.

tools.name: Figma MCP server for Claude Code
tools.cost: Free to add. Figma's free plan allows about 20 requests a month. The free Education plan for students allows 200 a day.
tools.dataAccess: The Figma files you link, read by Claude Code when you ask.
tools.why: Claude can read the real frames, layers and styles instead of guessing from a screenshot.

setup.command: claude mcp add --scope user --transport http figma https://mcp.figma.com/mcp
steps: Add the Figma server to Claude Code.
In Claude Code, type /mcp, pick figma, choose Authenticate, then click Allow access in the browser.
Copy a link to a Figma frame and paste it into your prompt.

design: Select a frame in Figma and copy its link.
In Claude Code, paste the link and ask it to build or critique that frame.
Ask it to use your Figma styles and variables by name.

tools.name: Figma Make
tools.cost: Included in Figma. The free plan gives 500 AI credits a month, up to 150 a day.
tools.dataAccess: The frames and prompts you give it, inside your Figma account.
tools.why: Turns a prompt or a frame into a clickable prototype, inside Figma.
tools.coachLine: You have Figma, and Figma Make can turn a frame into a working prototype from a prompt.

steps: Open Figma and start a Make file.

design: Start a Make file and paste in a frame.
Describe what should happen when someone clicks.
Test it, then ask for one change at a time.

tools.name: Claude Code
tools.cost: Needs a paid Claude plan or API credits
tools.dataAccess: The files in the folder you run it in, sent to Anthropic when it works on them.
tools.why: Works across your whole project. Good for learning, since you can ask it to explain each change.

steps: Install Claude Code.
Open Terminal in your project folder and type claude.
Sign in when it asks.

coding: Open Terminal in your project folder and type claude.
Describe the change you want in plain words.
Read the diff before you accept it, and ask why when something looks odd.

tools.name: Cursor
tools.cost: Free plan with limited agent requests. Paid plans run from $8 to $200 a month.
tools.dataAccess: The code in the folder you open, sent to Cursor's servers when the AI works on it.
tools.why: A code editor with an AI agent built in. Familiar if you've used VS Code.
tools.coachLine: You have Cursor, but you haven't opened it lately. Its agent can make this change for you.

steps: Install Cursor.
Open your project folder in it.

coding: Open the agent panel and describe the change.
Review each file it touched before you accept.

tools.name: Codex
tools.cost: The Codex CLI comes with ChatGPT Plus and up. Free and Go plans get lighter Codex use in the ChatGPT desktop app.
tools.dataAccess: The files in the folder you run it in, sent to OpenAI when it works on them.
tools.why: OpenAI's coding agent. A good fit if you already pay for ChatGPT.

steps: Install Codex.
Open Terminal in your project folder and type codex.
Sign in with your ChatGPT account.

coding: Open Terminal in your project folder and type codex.
Describe the change in plain words.
Review the diff before you accept it.
